item.title: Should Judges Campaign? Kansas Just Voted on the Last Bar-Controlled Court in America
item.body:
On Tuesday, August 4, Kansas voters weighed in on a question most states settled generations ago: who should get to pick the people who decide what the state constitution means?

The measure on the ballot — Amendment 1 — would abolish the Kansas Supreme Court Nominating Commission, the body that has screened candidates for the state's highest court since 1958, and replace the entire appointment process with direct statewide elections. It is a structural change, not a policy one. But almost nobody in Kansas has been arguing about it in structural terms.

Here is what was actually on the ballot, how Kansas ended up as an outlier, and why a fight over judicial paperwork became one of the most heavily contested items on an August primary ballot.

---

## What the amendment would actually do

The proposal is short, and its mechanics matter more than the slogans on either side.

- **It eliminates the nominating commission.** The nine-member body that currently vets applicants and forwards names to the governor would cease to exist.
- **It replaces appointment with election.** All seven justices would be chosen by Kansas voters statewide.
- **Terms stay at six years**, but the ballot cycle is staggered: positions 1, 2 and 3 would be elected in November 2028; positions 4 and 5 in 2030; positions 6 and 7 in 2032; and every six years after that.
- **The Legislature decides the format.** The amendment itself does not specify whether judicial races would be partisan (with party labels on the ballot) or nonpartisan. That call would be left to lawmakers in a future session — a detail that became a significant point of contention during the campaign.
- **Restrictions on judicial political activity would be repealed.** Provisions in Article 3 of the Kansas Constitution limiting justices' party involvement and campaign fundraising would come off the books, since a candidate for office needs to be able to campaign.

Nothing would change immediately. Even under approval, the first election under the new system would not occur until November 2028, and sitting justices would hold their seats until the scheduled election for their position.

---

## The system Kansas has now

Under the current process, a vacancy on the Kansas Supreme Court triggers a three-step sequence.

First, the Supreme Court Nominating Commission reviews applicants and selects three finalists. Second, the governor must appoint one of those three — the governor cannot go outside the list, and if the governor does not act within the constitutional window, the appointment authority passes to the chief justice. There is no confirmation vote by the Kansas Senate. Third, the new justice faces a yes-or-no retention election at the next general election after serving at least a year, and again every six years.

The commission itself is where Kansas stands alone. It has nine members: **five attorneys elected by members of the Kansas bar** — one from each congressional district plus a chairperson elected statewide by lawyers — and **four non-attorneys appointed by the governor**.

That five-to-four split is the whole controversy in one line. Roughly 21 states use some form of nominating commission. Kansas is the only one in which the state bar selects a majority of the commissioners, meaning the licensed legal profession, rather than any elected official, holds the deciding votes on who reaches the shortlist.

---

## How Kansas got here

The 1958 design was itself a reform, and a reaction to a specific scandal.

In the mid-1950s, Governor Fred Hall lost his party's primary. Shortly before his term ended, a vacancy opened on the Supreme Court. Hall resigned, his lieutenant governor was sworn in as governor, and the new governor promptly appointed Hall to the court. Kansas newspapers called it the "Triple Play," and the backlash was immediate. Two years later, voters approved the commission system specifically to take raw appointment power away from a governor acting alone.

That history is why both sides in 2026 could claim to be the reformers. Supporters of the amendment argue the 1958 fix created a different concentration of power — one held by an unelected professional guild. Opponents argue the fix worked exactly as designed and that dismantling it invites the problem it was built to prevent.

Nationally, Kansas would not be doing anything exotic by switching. Roughly 21 states already elect their supreme court justices — about 13 through nonpartisan races and eight through partisan ones. Kansas would become the 22nd.

---

## Why the vote happened now

The proximate trigger was a line of rulings, and one in particular.

In 2019, the Kansas Supreme Court held that Section 1 of the Kansas Constitution's Bill of Rights protects a right to personal autonomy that includes decisions about abortion — a ruling that made the state constitution, not the Legislature, the controlling document on the issue. In August 2022, voters rejected a proposed amendment that would have reversed that interpretation, by roughly 59% to 41% in a primary election that drew unusually heavy turnout. That November, all six justices on the retention ballot were retained, with support ranging from about 65% to 73%.

After 2022, Attorney General Kris Kobach publicly urged legislators to put judicial selection itself before voters. In 2025, they did. Senate Concurrent Resolution 1611 cleared the Kansas Senate 27–13 and the House 84–40 — in both chambers, exactly the two-thirds minimum required to refer a constitutional amendment. Every yes vote came from a Republican. Counting both chambers, about 93% of Republicans who voted supported it; no Democrat did.

Lawmakers also chose to place the question on the August primary ballot rather than the November general election. Supporters argued the measure deserved its own spotlight and pointed to 2022 as proof that Kansans turn out for constitutional questions. Critics argued August primaries usually draw a smaller and less representative electorate.

---

## The argument, taken seriously on both sides

Strip away the campaign advertising and there are two coherent positions.

**The case for elections.** Judicial decisions are, unavoidably, exercises in judgment about contested values. If a court is going to make consequential calls on constitutional meaning, the people affected should have direct say over who sits there. The current design gives a self-selecting professional group — several thousand licensed attorneys — a structural majority over a shortlist the governor cannot depart from. That is real public power with no electoral check attached. Retention elections, supporters note, almost never remove anyone; no Kansas Supreme Court justice has lost one.

**The case against.** Courts are supposed to be the branch that can rule against the majority. A judge who must raise money and win a statewide race faces incentives every other candidate faces, and those incentives point toward the interests funding the race. Because judges eventually rule on cases involving their own donors, elected courts create recusal problems that appointed courts do not. Opponents also point to the amendment's silence on partisan versus nonpartisan format: voters were asked to approve a change whose most consequential detail would be filled in later by the Legislature.

The unresolved question sitting underneath both arguments is money. Statewide judicial races in other states have drawn tens of millions of dollars in recent cycles, much of it from out-of-state groups on both sides. Kansas would be adding seven such races to its calendar on a rolling basis. Whether that counts as democratic accountability or as a new pressure on the bench is not a factual dispute — it is a genuine disagreement about what courts are for.

---

## Who lined up where

Backing the amendment: the Kansas Republican Party, the Kansas Chamber, Americans for Prosperity–Kansas, Attorney General Kris Kobach, and former Governor Jeff Colyer.

Opposing it: Governor Laura Kelly, a term-limited Democrat; former Republican Governor Bill Graves and former Democratic Governor Kathleen Sebelius; several former Kansas Supreme Court justices, including a former chief justice who publicly urged a no vote; the Kansas Bar Association; the Kansas Association of School Boards; the ACLU of Kansas; and Kansas Appleseed.

The bipartisan character of the opposition — and the near-total party-line character of the legislative support — is itself part of the story either side tells about the measure.

---

## What happens next

Election-night tallies in Kansas are unofficial. County boards canvass results in the days following the election, and the state canvass certifies the final figures later in the month. Official totals for Amendment 1 come out of that process.

**If it is approved**, the commission is abolished and Kansas moves to elected justices, with the first races in November 2028. The Legislature would then need to pass implementing law — most importantly, deciding partisan versus nonpartisan ballots, and setting rules for judicial campaign finance and recusal.

**If it is rejected**, nothing changes. The commission continues, the governor keeps appointing from three names, retention elections continue on the existing schedule, and Kansas remains the only state where the bar holds a majority on the body that picks the finalists.

---

## The larger question

The Kansas vote is a local decision with a national subtext. Every state has to answer the same question somehow: courts need enough independence to rule against popular majorities, and enough legitimacy that the public accepts those rulings. Appointment systems buy independence and risk looking insular. Elections buy legitimacy and risk turning the bench into another campaign.

There is no arrangement that delivers both without cost. What Kansas voters were asked on Tuesday was not which system is perfect, but which trade-off they would rather live with — and, more bluntly, who they trust to pick the referees.

---

### Quick facts

| | |
|---|---|
| **Vote date** | August 4, 2026 (primary ballot) |
| **Current system** | Nominating commission → governor appoints from 3 names → retention elections |
| **Commission makeup** | 5 attorneys elected by the bar, 4 non-attorneys appointed by the governor |
| **Proposed system** | Direct statewide election, 6-year terms |
| **First elections if approved** | Positions 1–3 in 2028; 4–5 in 2030; 6–7 in 2032 |
| **Legislative vote** | Senate 27–13, House 84–40 — the exact two-thirds minimum in both chambers |
| **National context** | ~21 states already elect justices; Kansas would be the 22nd |

*This article is a general explainer on state judicial selection and does not offer legal advice or endorse a position on the measure. For certified vote totals and official ballot language, consult the Kansas Secretary of State.*
